blocks.html: A mean combines every value in a dataset into one number by a stated combining rule. “The mean” means the arithmetic mean (§2.2.1) unless a question says otherwise. Three variants exist for data with a different arithmetic structure: the weighted mean (§2.2.2) when observations count unequally, the geometric mean (§2.2.3) when values combine by multiplication, and the harmonic mean (§2.2.4) when you average rates whose numerators are fixed. Every mean needs arithmetic to be meaningful on the variable, so the data must be at least interval-scaled (recall §1.1.2.3); the geometric and harmonic means need more, namely strictly positive values on a ratio scale (recall §1.1.2.4). A mean is never valid on nominal or ordinal data.
Arithmetic Mean

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The arithmetic mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Add everything up and divide by how many things you added. Why is this “the” typical value? It is the single number that, if it replaced every observation, would leave the total unchanged. It is also the balance point: place each value as a weight on a seesaw, and the seesaw balances at the mean.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The balance-point property follows in two lines. Write the n values as x₁, x₂, …, xₙ (the small number below is a label: x₁ is the first value, not a power), and write Σ (“sigma”) for “add up”, so Σx = x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ. The deviations from x̄ are (x₁ − x̄), …, (xₙ − x̄). Their sum is

Σ(x − x̄) = Σx − n·x̄ = Σx − n·(Σx ÷ n) = 0.

So the positive and negative deviations cancel exactly, for any dataset.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Five children’s weights: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 kg. Sum = 55. Mean = 55 ÷ 5 = 11 kg. The deviations are −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, and they sum to 0, as the derivation promised.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: mean from grouped data
blocks.html:
When only the frequency table survives, each class is represented by its class mark (mid-point; recall §1.4.2), and each mark is counted as many times as its class frequency f. The mean is then Σ(f·x) ÷ Σf. Today’s 30 children (recall §1.4.1):

Class (kg) Mid-point x f f·x
8 to <10 9 5 45
10 to <12 11 12 132
12 to <14 13 9 117
14 to <16 15 4 60
Total 30 354
  1. Multiply each mid-point by its frequency (last column).
  2. Add: Σf·x = 354; Σf = 30.
  3. Grouped mean = 354 ÷ 30 = 11.8 kg.

The mean of the 30 raw weights is 11.81 kg. The grouped mean is close because the values inside each class sit roughly evenly around its mid-point; with wide or lopsided classes the two can differ more.

points.html: Formulas: sample mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n; population mean μ = Σx ÷ N; grouped mean = Σf·x ÷ Σf.

Defining property: Σ(x − x̄) = 0. This is why the average deviation from the mean is useless as a measure of spread, and why dispersion measures either take absolute values or square the deviations (§3.5, §3.6).
Every value pulls on the mean in proportion to its size, so one extreme value can drag it away from where most of the data sit. The median (§2.3) exists partly to resist this.

blocks.html: Weighted Mean

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The weighted mean is an arithmetic mean in which each value counts in proportion to an assigned weight w, rather than every value counting once.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The arithmetic mean assumes every observation deserves equal say. When some observations stand for more units of the thing you are averaging, that assumption is wrong. The weighted mean multiplies each value by its weight before adding, and divides by the total weight instead of a plain count.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
A health worker has the average household size in three villages: Village A (25 households, average size 4), Village B (100 households, average size 5), Village C (10 households, average size 3).

The unweighted mean (4 + 5 + 3) ÷ 3 = 4 gives tiny Village C the same say as Village B. The quantity wanted is the average size of a household in the district, so each village’s weight is its number of households:

Weighted mean = (25×4 + 100×5 + 10×3) ÷ (25 + 100 + 10) = 630 ÷ 135 ≈ 4.67

The weight must match the quantity being averaged. Had the question been “what household size does a randomly chosen person in the district live in?”, the weight would be the number of persons in each village, because a person is more likely to live in a large household. Both are legitimate weighted means; they answer different questions.

points.html: Formula: weighted mean = Σ(w·x) ÷ Σw. The arithmetic mean is the special case with every w = 1. The grouped mean in §2.2.1 is a weighted mean of the mid-points, with the frequencies as weights.

Choose the weight from the target quantity: households for a per-household quantity, persons for a per-person quantity. Never average area-level rates or percentages across areas of unequal size without asking which weight fits. Doing so gives small areas an unfair say and produces a misleading “average of averages”.

blocks.html: Geometric Mean

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The geometric mean (GM) of n positive values is the nth root of their product. It averages quantities that combine by multiplication, such as growth factors and ratios, and data whose logarithms are roughly symmetric, such as antibody titres.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A population that grows 10% one year and 20% the next has been multiplied by 1.10 and then by 1.20. The GM is the single factor that, applied every year, gives the same overall product.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Taking logarithms turns products into sums: log(x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ) = Σ log x. So

log GM = (1/n) × Σ log x, and GM = exp(mean of log x), where exp undoes the natural log: exp(ln x) = x (with logs to base 2 or 10, raise 2 or 10 to that power instead).

The GM is therefore the arithmetic mean on the log scale, converted back (“back-transformed”) to the original scale. This is how software computes it, and it is why the GM needs strictly positive values: the logarithm of zero or of a negative number does not exist.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Growth. A population’s growth factors over three years are 1.10, 1.20 and 1.05.

GM = ∛(1.10 × 1.20 × 1.05) = ∛1.386 ≈ 1.1149, an average annual growth of about 11.49%.

The arithmetic mean of the three percentages is (10 + 20 + 5) ÷ 3 = 11.67%, which overstates the compounded growth: 1.11667³ = 1.3924, more than the true product 1.386.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: geometric mean titre (GMT)
blocks.html:
Serum antibody titres are reported as reciprocals of doubling dilutions (1:16, 1:32, 1:64 …), and a few children respond far more strongly than the rest. Vaccine studies therefore log-transform titres and report the geometric mean titre (GMT); an Indian H1N1 vaccine trial, for example, used “log transformation of the data to calculate Geometric Mean Titers (GMTs)” (Kubavat et al., 2011). Take eight children’s reciprocal titres after a vaccine dose (illustrative values): 16, 32, 32, 64, 64, 128, 256, 1024.

  1. Take log₂ of each (each doubling adds 1): 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 10.
  2. Mean of the logs = 51 ÷ 8 = 6.375.
  3. Back-transform: GMT = 2^6.375 (2 raised to the power 6.375) ≈ 83 (a titre of about 1:83).
  4. Compare: arithmetic mean = 1616 ÷ 8 = 202; median = 64.

The single child at 1024 more than doubles the arithmetic mean. Without that child the arithmetic mean is 84.6, and the GMT falls from 83 to 58. The GMT sits near the middle of the doubling steps, where most children are. Any log base gives the same GMT; base 2 just makes the steps whole numbers.

points.html: Formula: GM = (x₁ × x₂ × … × xₙ)^(1/n) = exp(mean of ln x).

Uses: average growth factors (population growth, year-on-year rise in incidence), ratios, and positively skewed positive data such as antibody titres, parasite counts and many laboratory values, where the GM is the back-transformed mean of the logs.
Needs strictly positive, ratio-scale values. A GM of temperatures in °C, or of a variable that includes zeros, is meaningless.
GM ≤ arithmetic mean for the same positive data, equal only when all values are identical. This is a useful check when computing by hand.

blocks.html: Harmonic Mean

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The harmonic mean (HM) of n positive values is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of their reciprocals: HM = n ÷ Σ(1/x).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The HM is the right average for rates when the numerator of the rate is the same for every observation. The classic case is speed (distance ÷ time) over equal distances: you spend more time at the slower speed, so the slower speed deserves more weight than a plain average gives it.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
The honest average of any set of rates is total numerator ÷ total denominator. For speeds vᵢ over distances dᵢ, the time on leg i is dᵢ/vᵢ, so

overall speed = Σd ÷ Σ(d/v).

If every leg has the same distance d, the d’s cancel: overall speed = n·d ÷ (d·Σ(1/v)) = n ÷ Σ(1/v), which is the HM. If instead every leg has the same time t, overall speed = Σ(v·t) ÷ (n·t) = Σv ÷ n, the plain arithmetic mean.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: You drive 60 km at 30 km/h, then another 60 km at 60 km/h. The arithmetic mean of the speeds is 45 km/h, but the trip took 60/30 + 60/60 = 3 h for 120 km, so the true average is 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h. The HM gives 2 ÷ (1/30 + 1/60) = 2 ÷ 0.05 = 40 km/h. Had you instead driven one hour at each speed, you would have covered 90 km in 2 h, and the arithmetic mean, 45 km/h, would be correct.

points.html: Rule: equal numerators (same distance, same number of doses) → harmonic mean; equal denominators (same time, same population) → arithmetic mean. In general, use total numerator ÷ total denominator, which is a weighted mean of the rates with the denominators as weights.
For the same positive data, HM ≤ GM ≤ arithmetic mean, all equal only when every value is identical. These three are the “Pythagorean means”.
The HM is rarely named in community medicine, but the rule behind it recurs whenever rates are combined across groups.

questions.prompt: A district has three villages. Village P has 1,000 eligible children with 60% measles vaccination coverage; villages Q and R have 100 eligible children each, both with 95% coverage. Compute the unweighted mean of the three coverages and the district’s true coverage, and explain which weight you used.
questions.answer:
Unweighted mean = (60 + 95 + 95) ÷ 3 = 83.3%. This gives the two small villages two-thirds of the say, although they hold only 200 of the 1,200 eligible children.

Coverage is a per-child quantity, so weight each village by its number of eligible children: vaccinated = 0.60 × 1000 + 0.95 × 100 + 0.95 × 100 = 600 + 95 + 95 = 790; district coverage = 790 ÷ 1200 = 65.8%.

The unweighted mean overstates coverage by about 17.5 percentage points. This is total numerator ÷ total denominator, the weighted mean of §2.2.2.

questions.prompt: A population grew 10% one year and 20% the next. Compute the average annual growth rate with the geometric mean and compare it with the simple average of 10% and 20%.
questions.answer: Growth compounds: the population is multiplied by 1.10 and then by 1.20, a total factor of 1.32. GM = √(1.10 × 1.20) = √1.32 = 1.1489, so average growth is 14.9% per year. Check: 1.1489² = 1.32. The simple average is 15%, and 1.15² = 1.3225 overshoots the true 1.32. The gap is small here because the two rates are close. It widens as the rates differ more (GM ≤ AM, with equality only when all values are equal).

questions.prompt: An ASHA walks 12 km to a sub-centre at 4 km/h and returns the same 12 km by shared auto at 12 km/h. What is her average speed for the round trip, and which mean gives it directly?
questions.answer: Time out = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 h; time back = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 h. Average speed = 24 km ÷ 4 h = 6 km/h. The distances (the numerators of the speeds) are equal, so the harmonic mean gives it directly: HM = 2 ÷ (1/4 + 1/12) = 2 ÷ (4/12) = 6 km/h. The arithmetic mean, 8 km/h, is wrong because she spends three times as long at the slower speed.
